- .github/workflows/mark-stable.yml
Line or code reference: line 720 (`git ls-remote --exit-code origin "${tag_ref}" 2>/tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err`), and the diagnostic consumer at lines 738-740 (`[ -s /tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err ]` / `cat /tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err >&2`)
Problem: Every retry iteration writes the `git ls-remote` stderr to the same fixed path `/tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err`, which is then read back at the final-attempt diagnostic.
Why it fails at runtime: GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral, so a single job's three invocations of the helper for `$VERSION`, `stable`, and `$MAJOR` are sequential and would not collide. But the helper is a generic bash function and a self-hosted runner (or any future caller that runs the helper more than once concurrently, interleaved across two release jobs, or via `workflow_dispatch` while another job is mid-run) shares `/tmp` across processes. A second invocation overwrites the first's stderr between iterations, so when the first invocation reaches `[ "${attempt}" -eq "${max_attempts}" ]` and runs `cat /tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err >&2`, the file now belongs to the other invocation (wrong transport-failure text) or has been truncated to zero bytes (no diagnostic at all). The verification path uses `ls-remote`'s stdout and exit code, so functional correctness is preserved; the regression is in the diagnostic quality of the very failure the helper exists to surface.
SEVERITY: MAJOR
ISSUE_CONFIDENCE: 4

- tests/test_mark_stable_release_tag_refspec_contract.py
Line or code reference: lines 127-133 (`publication_environment = {**os.environ, "PUBLICATION_HELPER_CALL_LOG": ..., "PUBLICATION_HELPER_EXPECTED_OBJECT_ID": ..., "PUBLICATION_HELPER_MODE": ..., "PUBLICATION_HELPER_SCENARIO": ...}`)
Problem: The subprocess environment for the `bash -c` contract test inherits the entire parent environment verbatim, including `BASH_ENV` and `ENV`.
Why it fails at runtime: `tests/conftest.py` only scrubs the repo-pinning `GIT_*` variables from `os.environ` (lines around its GIT_* scrub block) and explicitly notes that per-test scrubs of `BASH_ENV` / `ENV` / `WORKSPACE_PATH` are the per-test responsibility. When `bash -c` is invoked in non-interactive mode, `BASH_ENV` is sourced as a startup file (the bash manual: "If this parameter is set when bash is executing a shell script, its value is interpreted as a filename containing commands to initialize the shell"); when `set -o posix` is in effect (or `POSIXLY_CORRECT=1` is set), `ENV` is sourced the same way. A referenced startup file that defines a `git` function or aliases `git=/usr/bin/git` shadows the test's mock `git()` shim — the helper then runs the real `git push` against the live checkout, the assertion matrix (push-success / remote-match / remote-conflict / remote-unreadable / remote-absent) collapses to real git semantics, and the test suite either hangs on a network call or reports a false negative. CI runners in this repo do not set `BASH_ENV` today, but a future operator who does (or any consumer-repo runner with a startup-file convention) silently breaks the contract. The fix is the same minimal scrub the conftest already applies for `GIT_*`: drop `BASH_ENV` / `ENV` (and the closely-related `BASH_FUNC_*` / `ENV` imports) before composing the dict, then overlay the four `PUBLICATION_HELPER_*` keys.
SEVERITY: MAJOR
ISSUE_CONFIDENCE: 4

Problem: The `publish_tag_with_remote_verification` helper writes `git ls-remote` stderr to the fixed path `/tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err`. On self-hosted runners where multiple jobs share a machine, concurrent invocations of this helper (or any other process) can clobber the file, producing misleading or missing diagnostic output on the final-attempt `cat`.
Why it fails at runtime: If two release jobs run concurrently on the same self-hosted runner, both write to the same `/tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err`. The final-attempt diagnostic `cat /tmp/release_tag_lsremote_err >&2` would display whichever invocation last wrote to the file, not the current invocation's stderr. The verification logic itself is unaffected (it uses stdout and exit code), but the diagnostic output is wrong.
